headlines.article_text: Meta stock sinks 8% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Meta stock sank 8% Thursday as free cash flow turned negative and the company raised the floor of its expected capex spend. Prices for the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs. Meta also revealed it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock. In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg tries on Orion AR glasses at the Meta Connect annual event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, U.S., September 25, 2024. Manuel Orbegozo | Reuters Meta shares slumped roughly 8% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures. The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans. Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion. Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter. The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth." Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing. Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted. Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable with the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for. — CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report. headlines.summary: Governments or companies looking for an alternative to SpaceX's Starlink are faced with few options, as Amazon, Eutelsat and others are far behind.
headlines.article_text: Elon Musk's Ukraine clash accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ukraine's problems with SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield have accelerated demand for alternative satellite internet services. Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have flared up after reports that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered speed limits on Starshield service in the country. Amazon, Eutelsat and sovereign operators have raced to build out constellations, but they have yet to catch up with SpaceX. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in the Zaporizhzhia region set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, Oct. 16, 2026. Dmytro Smolienko | Ukrinform | Future Publishing | Getty Images Elon Musk 's latest clash with Ukraine underscores the critical role that his company's Starlink satellite internet service has played in Kyiv's defense against Russia, which invaded unprovoked in 2022. It's also laid bare the downsides of depending on a single provider for satellite internet communications, though other options are not yet comparable to SpaceX's Starlink and its military-grade Starshield offering. On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself. SpaceX and the U.S., they said, had suddenly and without warning imposed speed limits on Starshield . SpaceX describes Starshield as a "secured satellite network for government entities" that "leverages Starlink technology." The changes cut wireless internet connectivity in drones and other aircraft moving at speeds over 100 mph that Ukrainian forces were using in the campaign against Russia. A Ukrainian senior commander told The New York Times the Starlink restrictions cost his unit more than $1 million and delayed missions by three days. Musk and President Donald Trump , both critics of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , have each shirked accountability for the communications disruptions in the war-torn nation. On Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk individually ordered the service changes, and had discussed them with Trump before putting them in place. Trump insisted on Wednesday that he "was not involved." Robert Weissman, who is co-president of watchdog group Public Citizen, said the situation is an "extreme danger " that raises antitrust and security concerns around Musk's ability to control a "crucial means of communication." "People worry about the political, as well as economic, impacts of oligarchy, and this is it," Weissman said in an interview. "It's not just that Musk can drown out other speakers, he can close down communications in a national security context for a country. No person should have that ability or power." watch now VIDEO 1:05 01:05 Pres. Trump: Don't know who ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, but 'I was not involved' Closing Bell: Overtime The disruptions have prompted a bipartisan group of lawmakers in the U.S. to call for an investigation into Musk's actions, including calls for him to potentially testify under oath. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC on Wednesday that he doesn't believe Musk would have acted "without at least the acquiescence of the White House," and called attempts to throttle Starlink service in Ukraine "frankly shameful." "There's a reason why we've had relative peace in Europe since World War II," Cornyn said in a " Squawk on the Street " interview. "And that's because of the alliance between the United States and our European allies. And I think anything we do to undermine that or degrade that is a big mistake." Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., called for an investigation on the matter and wrote, in a social media post Wednesday, "No billionaire, especially one that gets massive contracts from our government, should have the power to unilaterally decide to shut down communications and weapons during a war of critical importance to the US and Ukraine." headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: PG, LRCX, BX, LUV, TTMI Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out some of the companies making the biggest moves midday: American Airlines — The largest U.S. carrier by passengers added 3%. American plans to slow its capacity growth next year after forecasting deeper losses this year as record revenue fails to offset the spike in fuel costs. Southwest Airlines — The Dallas-based airline climbed 5%. Southwest now anticipates earning between $2.60 and $2.85 per share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its July call for $3.25 to $4.25 per share. Procter & Gamble — The Ivory soap and Tide detergent maker climbed 6% after beating on both the top and bottom lines in the fiscal first quarter. P & G saw adjusted earnings of $2.00 per share, topping the $1.88 consensus estimate, according to LSEG. Revenue totaled $23.28 billion, above the $22.80 billion expected from analysts. Forgent Power Solutions – The electrical distribution company plummeted 24% after announcing its finance chief Ryan Fiedler will step down from the post and transition to an external consulting role. Executive vice president of finance Amy Ard was appointed CFO to replace Fiedler. SAP SE — Shares of the German software company advanced 4% after third-quarter earnings and revenue topped analysts' estimates. Blackstone – The alternative asset manager gained 6% after third-quarter profit surpassed Wall Street's estimates. Adjusted earnings totaled $1.32 per share, while analysts polled by LSEG forecast $1.26 a share. Total assets under management hit $1.368 trillion. Comcast – The Universal theme parks owner advanced 4% after Comcast beat analysts' estimates in the third quarter. Adjusted earnings of $1.07 per share on revenue of $29.30 billion topped LSEG consensus estimates of 98 cents a share and $29.28 billion. Free cash flow of $4.21 billion also came in above the StreetAccount consensus of $3.32 billion. TTM Technologies — The printed circuit board maker plunged 28%. The midpoint of fourth-quarter per share earnings guidance missed the Street consensus by 1 cent, while the revenue forecast matched expectations, FactSet data showed. Hexcel — The Connecticut-based maker of composite materials for the aerospace industry slumped 11%. Third-quarter revenue, operating income, gross margin and operating margins all missed Street estimates, FactSet's StreetAccount service said. Aevex — The defense company rose more than 7% after it disputed a Bloomberg News report that said the U.S. Navy would no longer buy Aevex's GARC boat drone due to performance issues. In a release, Aevex said " no orders have been halted ." Lockheed Martin — Shares rose 5% after the prime defense contractor reported better-than-expected results for the third quarter. Lockheed also hiked earnings and revenue guidance. Spotify — The audio streaming service surged 9% on fourth-quarter revenue guidance that exceeded analyst expectations. Spotify also said monthly active users rose 11% to 788 million year over year . Energy stocks — Parts of the group rose as oil prices surged amid renewed geopolitical fears in the Middle East. Kinder Morgan climbed 4%. Meta Platforms — The Facebook parent dropped more than 7% after revenue came in ahead of analysts' estimates. Third-quarter revenue of $64.60 billion topped the LSEG consensus call for $63.37 billion. The midpoint of its fourth-quarter sales guidance was also above the Street's estimates. CSX — The railway climbed 7% after third-quarter results beat expectations.
